 Proposed SNAP Changes Would Remove Many Tennesseans From Roll 
 Trump administration seeks to limit newly implemented policy in the state 
 Hannah Herner 
 Hannah Herner

 A new federal attempt to limit SNAP benefits would cause “whiplash” for some Tennessee families, according to locally based health advocacy organization Tennessee Justice Center. 
 Earlier this month, the Trump administration released proposed changes to SNAP (the federal government’s Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) that would narrow a policy called broad-based categorical eligibility. 
 “It’s working families that received a small raise or moderate gain in their income that are going to be removed from SNAP,” says Anna Grace Dastugue, the Tennessee Justice Center’s director of nutrition policy. 
 These changes, if approved, would remove approximately 6.3 million people — or nearly 18 percent of recipients — from SNAP nationally.  Because SNAP enrollment also influences eligibility for other food ​aid programs, the USDA estimates that 1.8 million children would ​also lose eligibility for free school lunch. 
 Will Tennessee Figure Out a Grocery Tax This Legislative Session? 
 Legislation filed by Republican leadership would eliminate the currently existing tax on milk, eggs and bread
 In Tennessee, the newly implemented broad-based categorical eligibility expands access to SNAP by raising the gross monthly income level ceiling from 130 percent to 200 percent of the federal poverty level. A family of four can now make up to $5,500 per month and remain on the program, an increase from $3,575 per month. Tennessee’s program also removed the asset test, which allows people to have a savings account and still access SNAP benefits. 
 Tennessee was the 47th state to add such benefits, and Dastugue notes that the state just did so in May.
 “If you start receiving 25 cents more an hour, if you fell really close to that poverty line, then [broad-based categorical eligibility] helps those people stay connected to SNAP but just receive less benefits,” Dastugue tells the Scene . “It encourages work and allows people to have some progress in their careers and jobs and maintain SNAP,  because remember, we’re still talking about very, very low-income families that are receiving very, very low wages.” 
 If the changes are approved following a 30-day comment period, “It’s definitely going to cause some whiplash for DHS eligibility counselors and families,” Dastugue notes, “because they went from two very different SNAP rules in a matter of six months, essentially.”
 Dastugue says the SNAP program is still feeling the effects of the passage of the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill” in 2025 , with increased work requirements and more administrative fee burden. States pay 50 percent of administrative fees for SNAP, but under the new budget, states are required to pay for up to 75 percent of those costs starting in 2028. As a result, more than 5.5 million Americans in the past year have already lost coverage.  
 In addition, the Tennessee General Assembly sought to restrict the use of SNAP benefits on the purchase of sugary foods and soda in 2025 — an effort that was voided by a federal judge earlier this year .
